overview: Kanak communities in New Caledonia sustain diverse languages, clan relationships and connections to customary land. Their history continues through colonial disruption and contemporary cultural creativity.

items.text: Clan relationships connect shared land, narratives, responsibilities and chiefly authority. These local structures should not be collapsed into one island-wide kingdom.
Circular houses combine wood, lianas and thatch. Carved door frames and roof spires express relationships with lineages and ancestors.
Customary exchanges of words and gifts express respect and acknowledge relationships during visits and important occasions.
Community practices include cultivation, spearfishing, pandanus weaving, canoe making and carving. Workshops and local teaching carry these skills forward.
France claimed New Caledonia in 1853. Settler expansion later forced Indigenous communities onto reserves; these administrative changes did not end Kanak cultures.
The Tjibaou Cultural Centre presents Kanak and other Oceanian arts. Its Kanak path relates the story of Tea Kanake, linking contemporary interpretation with cultural narratives.
